walkthrough:
Set Up The Kidney Scene - The PCT Cell**
You are in the proximal convoluted tubule. The filtrate in the lumen still contains all the useful glucose, amino acids, vitamins and many $Na^+$ ions. Your job is to get them back to blood. The PCT cell has two sides: the apical side facing the lumen and the basal side facing blood. Remember active transport needs ATP and moves ions against their gradient.

How Sodium Drives Reabsorption By Cotransport**
On the basal membrane, sodium-potassium pumps actively transport $Na^+$ out of the PCT cell into the blood. That keeps $Na^+$ concentration very low inside the cell. So there is now a steep $Na^+$ gradient from lumen (high) to cell (low). $Na^+$ therefore moves down this gradient into the cell from the filtrate by facilitated diffusion through carrier proteins in the apical membrane. Those carriers cotransport glucose, amino acids or other ions at the same time. Once inside, glucose then diffuses down its own gradient out of the basal side into the blood. So sodium does not just get reabsorbed itself, it indirectly powers reabsorption of glucose.

Set Up The Synapse Scene - Arrival Of The Impulse**
Now jump to a cholinergic synapse, which uses acetylcholine (ACh). When an action potential arrives and depolarises the presynaptic membrane, this voltage change is the trigger. Voltage-gated calcium ion channels in the presynaptic membrane open. Because $Ca^{2+}$ concentration is higher outside than inside, $Ca^{2+}$ diffuses rapidly into the presynaptic bulb.

How Calcium Releases Transmitter**
The sudden rise in $Ca^{2+}$ inside acts as a signal to the synaptic vesicles full of ACh. The vesicles move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane. The membrane then opens to the cleft and ACh is released by exocytosis. Without that calcium influx, vesicle fusion and transmitter release would not happen.

Final answer: In PCT: $Na^+$ actively transported out of basal side of PCT cells into blood, lowering $Na^+$ concentration in cell and creating a concentration gradient. $Na^+$ enters cells from lumen/filtrate by facilitated diffusion via carrier proteins, cotransporting glucose/amino acids/ions. Glucose then diffuses into blood. In cholinergic synapse: depolarisation of presynaptic membrane opens voltage-gated $Ca^{2+}$ channels, $Ca^{2+}$ enters presynaptic neurone, causing ACh vesicles to move to/fuse with presynaptic membrane and release ACh by exocytosis.

walkthrough:
Build Paired Comparisons - Route And Signal**
Always answer compare in pairs: nervous on one side, endocrine on the other. Nervous communication uses action potentials or nerve impulses travelling along neurones, involving both electrical and chemical stages. Endocrine communication uses hormones, which are purely chemical messengers carried in the blood plasma. That one difference in route explains almost all the others.

Speed, Spread And Duration**
Because neurones provide a direct fast line, nervous transmission is fast, the response in muscle or gland is fast, but short-lived and highly specific or localised. Hormones must circulate in blood, so transmission is slower, the response is slower, but effects can be widespread across many target organs, tissues or cells and can be long-lasting or even permanent, for example in growth and development.

Targets, Receptors And Similarities**
Nervous responses act on effectors - muscles and glands - with neurotransmitter receptors on the postsynaptic cell surface membrane. Hormones act on target cells, with receptors either on the cell surface membrane or inside the cell, since steroid hormones can pass through membranes. Despite the differences, both are cell signalling systems: both use a chemical signal molecule that binds to a specific receptor to trigger a response.

Final answer: Differences: nervous - impulses/action potentials, electrical and chemical; endocrine - hormones, chemical only. Transmitted via neurones vs via blood. To specific muscle/gland vs to target organs/tissues/cells. Nervous faster transmission, faster response, short-lived; endocrine slower transmission, slower response, long-lasting, can be permanent. Nervous effects localised/specific; endocrine can be widespread. Receptors on cell surface membrane for nervous vs on surface membrane or inside cell for endocrine. Similarities: both involve cell signalling, signal molecule binding to receptor, both involve chemicals.
